What are the phases of the SDLC?

Requirements gathering and analysis, design (architecture, data model, APIs, UI), implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance. Waterfall executes them once in sequence; Agile repeats all of them in every short iteration so each sprint produces tested, potentially releasable software.
Waterfall vs Agile — when would you choose each?

Waterfall fits projects with stable, fully known requirements, fixed contracts or heavy regulatory sign-off, where predictability matters more than flexibility. Agile fits products where requirements evolve and early user feedback is valuable; it reduces risk by delivering working increments frequently. Its downside is less up-front predictability of final scope, which is managed through backlog prioritisation and forecasting from velocity.
What are the four values of the Agile Manifesto?

Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan. The right-hand items still have value — Agile just values the left-hand items more. 💡 Mention that "working software over documentation" does not mean no documentation.
What are the Scrum roles and what does each do?

The 2020 Scrum Guide calls them accountabilities. The Product Owner maximises value and owns and orders the Product Backlog. The Scrum Master is accountable for team effectiveness — coaching Scrum, removing impediments and serving the team and organisation. The Developers create a usable Increment each sprint and own the Sprint Backlog. There is no separate "team lead" or "QA" role in Scrum; testers are Developers too.
Walk through the Scrum events.

The Sprint is a fixed time-box of one month or less that contains all other events. Sprint Planning sets the Sprint Goal, selects backlog items and plans the work. The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute Developer event to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan. The Sprint Review inspects the Increment with stakeholders and adapts the Product Backlog. The Retrospective identifies improvements to process, tools, interactions and the Definition of Done.
Is the Daily Scrum a status meeting with the "three questions"?

Not necessarily. The 2020 Scrum Guide removed the three questions (what I did yesterday, what I'll do today, blockers); Developers may use any structure that focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan for the next day. It is for the Developers, not a report to a manager, and detailed problem solving happens after it with the relevant people.
What are the Scrum artifacts and their commitments?

Product Backlog — an ordered list of everything needed to improve the product; commitment: the Product Goal. Sprint Backlog — the Sprint Goal, the selected items and the plan to deliver them; commitment: the Sprint Goal. Increment — the sum of usable, done work; commitment: the Definition of Done.
What makes a good user story? Explain INVEST.

A good story delivers user value, is written from the user's perspective and has clear acceptance criteria. INVEST: Independent of other stories where possible, Negotiable (a conversation, not a contract), Valuable to a user or the business, Estimable, Small enough to finish in a sprint, and Testable. Split big stories vertically so each slice is deployable end to end.
How do you write acceptance criteria? What is Given/When/Then?

Acceptance criteria are specific, testable conditions a story must satisfy, agreed by the PO, developers and QA before work starts. Given/When/Then (Gherkin, from BDD) structures each scenario: Given the precondition/context, When an action happens, Then the expected outcome. Include negative and edge cases. They translate directly into automated API or UI tests.
What are story points and why not estimate in hours?

Story points are a relative measure combining effort, complexity and uncertainty. Relative sizing ("this is about twice that one") is faster and more consistent than absolute hour estimates, works regardless of who picks up the task, and naturally accounts for risk. Velocity then converts points to a sprint forecast. Points should not be converted back into hours or used to compare individuals or teams.
How does planning poker work?

The PO explains a story, each estimator privately chooses a Fibonacci card, and everyone reveals simultaneously. If estimates differ widely, the highest and lowest voters explain their reasoning — often revealing missed complexity or a simpler approach — and the team re-votes until it converges. Simultaneous reveal prevents anchoring on the most senior person's number.
Definition of Ready vs Definition of Done vs acceptance criteria?

Definition of Ready is an optional team agreement on when a backlog item is clear enough to start (criteria written, dependencies known, estimated). Definition of Done is required in Scrum and is the shared quality standard for every Increment (reviewed, tested, merged, deployable, documented). Acceptance criteria are story-specific functional conditions. A story is done only when it meets both its acceptance criteria and the DoD.
What is Kanban and what are WIP limits for?

Kanban is a flow-based method that visualises work on a board, limits work in progress, and optimises flow without fixed iterations. WIP limits cap how many items can be in a column at once; when a column is full, the team helps finish work downstream instead of starting new work. This shortens cycle time, exposes bottlenecks such as slow code reviews, and reduces context switching.
Scrum vs Kanban — how do they differ?

Scrum uses fixed-length sprints, defined accountabilities, events and a sprint commitment; changes usually wait for the next sprint. Kanban has continuous flow, no prescribed roles or iterations, and items can be reprioritised at any time, governed by WIP limits. Scrum measures velocity; Kanban measures lead time, cycle time and throughput. Support and maintenance teams often prefer Kanban; product feature teams often use Scrum or a Scrumban hybrid.
Describe a typical Jira workflow you follow as a developer.

Pick a ready story from the sprint, move it to In Progress, create a branch named with the ticket key, commit with the key in the message, open a PR and move the ticket to In Review. After approval and merge, CI deploys to QA and the ticket moves to QA/Testing; QA verifies and moves it to Done or reopens it with a linked bug. Blockers are flagged immediately and raised in the Daily Scrum.
What is good code review etiquette?

As an author: small focused PRs, a clear description with the ticket link and how it was tested, and a self-review before requesting others. As a reviewer: review promptly, focus on correctness, design, security, tests and readability, critique the code not the person, explain why, and label minor points as nits or suggestions so they do not block. Let linters and Sonar handle formatting. 💡 Ask questions ("What happens if this list is empty?") instead of issuing commands.
How do you handle a hotfix for a critical production bug?

Reproduce or confirm the issue and mitigate first if possible (rollback, toggle a feature flag off). Branch from the production release tag, make the minimal fix plus a regression test, get an expedited review, run targeted tests on staging, deploy, and verify in production with monitoring. Then merge the hotfix back into the main/develop branch, bump the patch version, update the ticket and stakeholders, and hold a blameless post-mortem.
How do you approach production support issues?

Acknowledge quickly, assess severity and business impact, and communicate an initial status. Restore service first, then investigate root cause using logs, metrics, traces and correlation IDs, and check recent deployments or config changes. Document the fix, add tests, alerts or runbook steps so it does not recur, and log follow-up work in the backlog. Calm, clear communication matters as much as the technical fix.
What is velocity and how can it be misused?

Velocity is the average story points a team completes per sprint, used to forecast how much fits in future sprints. It is misused when management compares teams (points are team-relative) or sets velocity targets, which leads to point inflation instead of more value. Use a rolling average of the last three to five sprints for planning only.
Burndown vs burnup chart?

A burndown shows remaining work falling towards zero; if scope is added the line flattens and you can't tell why. A burnup plots completed work and total scope as separate lines, so scope changes are visible. Burnups are better for release tracking with stakeholders.
What is a spike?

A time-boxed story to investigate an unknown, such as testing whether a library handles HL7/FHIR messages or prototyping a payment integration, so the team can estimate or decide. It has a clear question and a time box (for example two days) and produces findings or a decision, not shippable code.
How do you handle technical debt in an Agile team?

Make it visible as backlog items that explain the cost to the business ("each release needs two days of manual regression"), let the Product Owner prioritise them alongside features, reserve a share of each sprint's capacity, and include quality items in the Definition of Done so new debt isn't created. Refactor code you are already changing rather than planning big rewrites.
The PO wants to add an urgent story mid-sprint. What happens?

The sprint goal should not be endangered. The team and PO negotiate: if the new item is truly urgent, something of similar size is removed from the sprint. If the change makes the sprint goal obsolete, only the PO can cancel the sprint. Genuine production incidents go through the support/hotfix process. Repeated mid-sprint changes are a topic for the retrospective (shorter sprints or Kanban may fit better).
The team didn't finish its sprint commitment. What do you do?

Unfinished items go back to the Product Backlog and are re-prioritised; they are not shown as done and partial points are not counted. In the retrospective, look for causes such as poor splitting, hidden dependencies, unplanned work or over-commitment, and agree concrete actions. The sprint goal is a commitment to a goal, not a guarantee of every item.
GitFlow vs trunk-based development?

GitFlow uses long-lived develop and release branches, suited to versioned, scheduled releases, but it creates merge pain and slows feedback. Trunk-based development merges small changes into main at least daily with strong CI and feature flags, enabling continuous delivery. Most web teams now use trunk-based or GitHub Flow with short-lived branches.
Blue-green vs canary deployment?

Blue-green runs two full environments and switches all traffic at once, so rollback is a single switch but it costs double infrastructure. Canary sends a small percentage of real traffic to the new version and increases it while monitoring metrics, limiting the blast radius of a bad release. Both need backward-compatible database migrations.
What are feature flags and their risks?

Feature flags turn functionality on or off at runtime, so code can be deployed dark and released to selected users, tested in production, or killed instantly. Risks: combinatorial testing paths, stale flags cluttering code, and security if flags are evaluated only in the front end. Give each flag an owner and an expiry and remove it after rollout.
What are the DORA metrics?

Four measures of software delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time for changes (commit to production), change failure rate (share of deployments causing incidents) and time to restore service. High performers deploy often with low failure rates, showing speed and stability reinforce each other through automation, small batches and good testing.
